title: Sounds and Script
description: The four things Punjabi does that English does not. Do this first if you want to be understood — or skip ahead to Unit 1 and come back.

lessons.title: The puff of air
lessons.goal: Hear and make the difference between k and kh, p and ph, t and th, ch and chh.
notes: English has both sounds already, but uses them at random: the p in 'pin' has a puff of air, the p in 'spin' does not. English speakers never notice, because swapping them never changes a word.
In Punjabi that puff is the whole word. pal is a moment; phal is fruit. Get it wrong and you have said a different thing.
Test yourself: hold a strip of paper in front of your mouth. On phal it should jump. On pal it should barely move.
These four pairs are all voiceless. The letters gh, jh, dh, bh look like the same idea but behave completely differently — they are tone letters, and they get their own lesson.

items.say: No puff. Like the p in 'spin', not 'pin'.
Strong puff of air after the p. Not an f.
Tongue on the teeth, no puff.
Same tongue position, then a puff. Never the 'th' of 'think'.
Like 'ch' in 'chair', no puff.
Same 'ch', then a clear puff of air.
Like the k in 'skill'. No puff.
Like the k in 'kill', with the puff exaggerated.

lessons.title: Where your tongue goes
lessons.goal: Separate the dental sounds from the retroflex ones — the single biggest giveaway of an English accent.
notes: English t and d are made with the tongue on the ridge behind the teeth — halfway between the two Punjabi sounds, and wrong for both.
Dental (t, d, n): push the tongue tip flat against the back of your upper front teeth. Softer and duller than English.
Retroflex (tt, dd, nn, rh): curl the tongue tip back and up, touching the roof of the mouth. Sharper and hollower than English.
If you use the English sound for both, Punjabi speakers will usually still understand you — but this is the thing that marks you out most, and it is fixable in an afternoon.

items.say: Dental: tongue flat on the back of the upper teeth.
Retroflex: tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth.
Dental d, tongue on the teeth.
Retroflex d, tongue curled back. Closer to the English d than the dental one is.
A tapped r, tongue forward.
Retroflex flap: curl the tongue back and flick it forward.
Ordinary tapped r.
That same backward flick of the curled tongue.

lessons.title: Tone, doubling and nasals
lessons.goal: Understand the three features that no amount of listening to a synthesiser will teach you.
notes: PUNJABI IS TONAL — almost alone among the languages of the region. The letters gh, jh, dh, dhh and bh are no longer pronounced as voiced aspirates. They lost the breath and gained a pitch: the syllable starts low and rises.
So ghorha (horse) is really pronounced closer to 'korha' with a dipping pitch, and korha (whip) is said flat. Same consonant, different melody, different word.
The addak — the little v-shape above a letter — doubles the consonant that follows it. Hold that consonant a beat longer: pata (knowledge) versus patta (leaf); sat (truth) versus satt (seven).
The bindi (a dot above) and tippi (a curl above) both nasalise: let air out through the nose while you say the vowel, as in the French 'bon'.

Be warned: this app's built-in voice is a synthesiser. It handles the puff and the tongue position well, but it under-plays tone and ignores doubling completely. For these three, trust the written explanation over what you hear — and copy a native speaker when you get the chance.

items.say: Flat, level pitch across the word.
Starts like k, but the pitch dips low then rises. Not a hard 'g'.
Single t, said quickly.
Hold the t: pat-ta. The addak doubles it.
Short and single.
Lean on the t. This is the word you met in Unit 3.
The bindi nasalises the vowel. The n is not a separate sound — it colours the aa.
The tippi nasalises before the b. Hum through the nose into the b.
